lead: A transformer reads all tokens of a sentence at once. Self-attention lets each token look at every other token, so a word's vector depends on the whole sentence. This removes the step-by-step bottleneck of an RNN from 6.2. BERT and GPT are two large pretrained transformers. BERT reads both directions and is fine-tuned for classification or span tasks. GPT reads left to right and is fine-tuned or prompted to generate text. Search engines, mail filters, chatbots and translation tools use these models.
prereq: You need: attention from 6.3, softmax from 6.1, and word vectors from Unit 5.

blocks.text: Self-attention turns each token vector into three vectors: a query Q, a key K and a value V. A learned matrix makes each one from the input. The query asks what this token needs. The key says what each token offers. The value carries the content that is passed on. For n tokens, Q, K and V are n × d<sub>k</sub> matrices. d<sub>k</sub> is the query/key width.

blocks.where: Q is the query matrix, K is the key matrix, V is the value matrix, d<sub>k</sub> is the key width. QK<sup>T</sup> holds one dot-product score per token pair; softmax turns each row of scores into weights that sum to 1.

blocks.text: The score q·k measures how much one token should listen to another. The dot product grows with d<sub>k</sub>, so dividing by √d<sub>k</sub> keeps the softmax from saturating. The weights multiply V. Each output row is a weighted sum of all value rows. Every token is computed in parallel, so a GPU can process a whole batch of sentences.

One attention head learns one kind of relation. Multi-head attention runs h heads in parallel, each with its own learned projections. The h outputs are concatenated and projected back to the model width. A head may track subject-verb links; another may track nearby words. The model learns these roles; they are not hand-coded.

Self-attention has no sense of order. Token 1 and token 5 get the same treatment if their vectors are the same. A positional encoding fixes this. It is a vector added to each token embedding. The original transformer uses fixed sine and cosine waves of different frequencies. Learned position vectors are also common. Addition, not concatenation, is the standard.

An encoder block has two sublayers. The first is multi-head self-attention. The second is a feed-forward network applied to each position separately. Each sublayer has a residual connection and layer normalisation: output = LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). The residual lets gradients flow through deep stacks. Layer norm keeps activations stable. The feed-forward part is usually two dense layers with a ReLU or GELU between them; it expands the width by about 4× and projects back.

A decoder block adds two changes. First, masked self-attention stops a position from seeing future tokens. The upper triangle of the score matrix is set to −∞ before softmax, so those weights become 0. Second, cross-attention takes queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder output. This is the same attention idea as 6.3, now inside each layer.

A stack of 6 to 12 such blocks is normal. Encoder-only stacks produce contextual vectors. Decoder-only stacks produce the next-token distribution. Encoder-decoder stacks are used for translation and summarisation; see 6.6.

BERT is an encoder-only transformer. It is pretrained on unlabelled text with masked language modelling. About 15 percent of tokens are chosen; 80 percent of those become [MASK], 10 percent become a random token and 10 percent stay unchanged. The model predicts the original token from both sides. A second objective, next-sentence prediction, asks whether sentence B follows sentence A. Special tokens mark the input: [CLS] at the start and [SEP] between sentences. The final [CLS] vector is used for classification. Unlike Word2Vec or FastText, a BERT vector for “bank” changes with the sentence.

Fine-tuning adds a small task head. For sentiment, a dense layer maps the [CLS] vector to positive or negative. For question answering, two vectors score the start and end of an answer span; see 6.7. The whole BERT stack is updated with a small learning rate. This is cheaper than pretraining from scratch.

GPT is a decoder-only transformer. It uses a causal mask and is trained to predict the next token at every position. The loss is the negative log-likelihood of the true next token. After pretraining, GPT can be fine-tuned on a labelled task or used by prompting. It generates text one token at a time; decoding is covered in 6.5. RoBERTa is a BERT variant trained longer without next-sentence prediction; DistilBERT is a smaller, faster BERT.

spec.title: One transformer encoder layer
spec.aria: A transformer encoder layer: embeddings plus positions go through multi-head self-attention, a residual add-and-normalise, a feed-forward network, another add-and-normalise, giving contextual vectors.

examples.question: One query attends over two keys with d<sub>k</sub> = 2. q₁ = [1,0], k₁ = [1,0], k₂ = [0,1], v₁ = [1,1], v₂ = [0,1]. Compute the attention output.
steps: Scores: q₁·k₁ = 1×1 + 0×0 = 1. q₁·k₂ = 1×0 + 0×1 = 0. The score row is [1, 0].
examples.answer: The attention output is [0.670, 1.000], with weights [0.670, 0.330].
examples.check:
import math
q=[1,0]
k1=[1,0]
k2=[0,1]
v1=[1,1]
v2=[0,1]
s1=sum(a*b for a,b in zip(q,k1))
s2=sum(a*b for a,b in zip(q,k2))
scaled1=s1/math.sqrt(2)
scaled2=s2/math.sqrt(2)
e1=math.exp(scaled1)
e2=math.exp(scaled2)
z=e1+e2
w1=e1/z
w2=e2/z
o1=w1*v1[0]+w2*v2[0]
o2=w1*v1[1]+w2*v2[1]
print(f'{w1:.3f}')
print(f'{w2:.3f}')
print(f'{o1:.3f}')
print(f'{o2:.3f}')

traps: BERT is encoder-only and GPT is decoder-only. BERT cannot generate left to right.
The scale √d<sub>k</sub> is applied inside the softmax, to the scores, not to the final output.
Positional encodings are added to token embeddings, not concatenated.
Masked self-attention belongs to the decoder. An encoder uses unmasked self-attention.
Next-sentence prediction is a BERT pretraining objective, not a GPT objective.

quiz.q: What are Q, K and V in self-attention?
quiz.a: Q is the query matrix, K is the key matrix and V is the value matrix. Each is made from the input by a learned projection.

quiz.q: Why are attention scores divided by √d<sub>k</sub>?
quiz.a: Dot products grow with d<sub>k</sub>. Large scores make softmax saturate, so one weight becomes almost 1. Dividing by √d<sub>k</sub> keeps the scores in a stable range.

quiz.q: A score row is [2, 0] and d<sub>k</sub> = 1. Compute the softmax weights.
Why can a BERT encoder not be used for left-to-right generation without a decoder?
quiz.a: BERT is trained with bidirectional masking and has no causal mask. Every position sees future tokens. It does not learn the next-token distribution needed for generation.

quiz.q: What does the causal mask do in a decoder?
quiz.a: It sets scores for future positions to −∞ before softmax. Their weights become 0, so position i can attend only to positions 1 to i.

quiz.q: What is the [CLS] vector used for in BERT classification?
quiz.a: The final [CLS] vector is a summary of the input pair. A dense classification head maps it to class scores.

quiz.q: A BERT input has 128 tokens. About how many tokens are chosen for masking at 15 percent?
A team must classify 10,000 support tickets into 20 categories and has 500 labelled examples. Choose BERT or GPT and justify.
quiz.a: Use BERT. It is encoder-only and gives a contextual [CLS] vector. Fine-tune a 20-way classification head on the 500 labels. GPT is decoder-only and is better suited to generation or prompting.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern retrieval systems use bi-encoders and cross-encoders built on BERT. Efficient variants replace self-attention with sparse or linear attention for long documents. Sentence-BERT and E5 produce sentence embeddings for search and clustering. Vision transformers apply the same block to image patches. Search terms: scaled dot-product attention, masked language modelling, causal language modelling, LoRA fine-tuning, FlashAttention.
